---
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:recursive axiomatizability}
    Is $\mathsf{ML}$ recursively axiomatizable? Equivalently, is $\mathsf{ML}$ decidable?
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob: coincidence problem}
    Does the inclusion $\mathsf{ML}\subseteq\mathsf{Skvo}$ hold?
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- problem-3: body_md -->
\label{prob: skortsov logic decidability}
    Does the logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ have the finite model property? Is it decidable?
<!-- end problem-3 -->
<!-- problem-4: body_md -->
\label{prob: decidability of modal medvedev}
    Is the logic $\mathsf{ML}_{\boxempty}$ recursively axiomatizable? Equivalently, is $\mathsf{ML}_{\boxempty}$ decidable?
<!-- end problem-4 -->
<!-- problem-5: body_md -->
\label{prob: modal skortsov logic decidability}
    Is $\mathsf{Skvo}_\boxempty$ decidable?
<!-- end problem-5 -->
<!-- problem-6: body_md -->
\label{prob: yankov axiomatizability}
    Are the logics $\mathsf{ML}$ or $\mathsf{ML}_{\boxempty}$ axiomatizable by Yankov formulas?
<!-- end problem-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
The logic $\mathsf{ML}$ is undecidable. In particular, it encodes a periodic tiling problem.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
The logic $\mathsf{ML}_{\boxempty}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
If $\mathsf{ML}_{\boxempty}$ was decidable, a decidability algorithm for $\mathsf{ML}$ would follow, by computing the translation $\sigma(\varphi)$ of any formula.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
The schematic fragment of inquisitive logic $\mathsf{Inq}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
The internal propositional logic of the presheaf topos $\mathbf{sSet}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
The logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is strictly contained in $\mathsf{ML}$. In particular, there is a formula $\rho_{\mathcal{W}}$, associated to a periodic set of tiles, such that $\rho_{\mathcal{W}}\in \mathsf{ML}\setminus \mathsf{Skvo}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
The logics $\mathsf{Skvo}$ and $\mathsf{Skvo}_\boxempty$ are both undecidable. In particular they encode a (non-periodic) tiling problem.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A bounded lattice $(H,\leq)$ is called a \emph{Heyting algebra} if for each $a,b\in H$, there is $a\rightarrow b\in H$ such that for each $c\in H$
    \begin{equation*}
        a\wedge c\leq b\iff c\leq a\rightarrow b.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Given a poset $P$, the \emph{upset algebra} of $P$ is the Heyting algebra $(\mathsf{Up}(P),\cap,\cup,\varnothing,P,\rightarrow)$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
An order-preserving map $f\colon P\to Q$ is called a \emph{p-morphism} if for all $p\in P$, and $q\in Q$ whenever $f(p)\leq q$ then there is some $p'\geq p$ such that $f(p')=q$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
If $f\colon P\to Q$ is a p-morphism, then $f^{-1}\colon \mathsf{Up}(Q)\to \mathsf{Up}(P)$ is a complete Heyting algebra homomorphism.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop: finite Esakia duality}
    The functors $\mathsf{Up}$ and $\mathsf{Spec}_{\infty}$ define a dual equivalence.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Given a Heyting algebra $H$ we say that an element $o\in H$ is the \emph{opremum} if $o$ is the second largest element of $H$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
It is well-known \cite[A.1.2]{Esakiach2019HeyAlg} that a Heyting algebra is subdirectly irreducible if and only if it has an opremum. Moreover, under Esakia duality, a finite Heyting algebra $H$ is subdirectly irreducible if and only if $\mathsf{Spec}(H)$ is rooted. We will make free use of this in what follows.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a finite subdirectly irreducible Heyting algebra, with $o$ its opremum, and let $D\subseteq A^{2}$, called the \emph{closed domain}. For each $a\in A$ we  introduce a variable $p_{a}$, and define,
\begin{align*}
\Delta(A,D) \coloneqq 
 & (p_{0}\leftrightarrow 0)\wedge (p_{1}\leftrightarrow 1) \wedge \bigwedge   \{p_{a\ast b}\leftrightarrow(p_a\ast p_b) : a,b\in A, \ast\in \{\wedge,\rightarrow\}\} \\
 &\wedge \bigwedge \{p_{a\vee b}\leftrightarrow(p_a\vee p_b) : (a,b)\in D\}.
\end{align*}
The \emph{canonical formula} associated with the pair $(A,D)$ is the formula:
\begin{equation*}
    \alpha(A,D)\coloneqq \Delta(A,D)\rightarrow p_{o}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
Using the duality of Proposition \ref{prop: finite Esakia duality} -- and by abuse of notation -- given a finite rooted poset $P$ and $D\subseteq \mathsf{Up}(P)^{2}$, we will write $\alpha(P,D)$ for the canonical formula $\alpha(\mathsf{Up}(P),D)$.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Several related classes of formulas are connected to canonical formulas.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For a finite subdirectly irreducible Heyting algebra $A$, a canonical formula $\alpha(A,D)$ is called a \emph{Yankov formula} whenever $D=A^{2}$. In such a case we denote the formula by $\mathcal{J}(H)$, or $\mathcal{J}(P)$ when referring to the associated finite poset.
        \item Canonical formulas exploit the local tabularity of the $(\wedge,\rightarrow,\top,\bot)$-fragment of $\mathsf{IPC}$, due to Diego \cite{Diego1966-DIESLA-5}. If instead one exploits the local tabularity of the $(\wedge,\vee,\top,\bot)$-fragment, the equivalent of canonical formulas are the \emph{stable canonical formulas}\cite{stablecanonicalformulas}. The choice to work with canonical formulas made here lies in the fact that these seem to make the definition of some maps in the reductions given in Section \ref{sec: undecidability of med} substantially easier.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop: algebraic criterion for validating canonical formulas}
    For each Heyting algebra $H$, and each finite subdirectly irreducible Heyting algebra $A$, with opremum $o$, and $D\subseteq A^{2}$ we have that $H\nvDash \alpha(A,D)$ if and only if there is a homomorphic image $H_{0}$ of $H$ a \emph{bounded implicative semilattice embedding}\footnote{Recall that such homomorphisms are those which preserve the $(\wedge,\rightarrow,0,1)$ subreduct.} $h\colon A\to H_{0}$, such that for each $(a,b)\in D$ we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        h(a\vee b)=h(a)\vee h(b).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
For every superintuitionistic logic $L$, $L$ is axiomatized by canonical formulas.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- notation-2: body_md -->
Given $P$ a poset, $Q$ a finite poset and let $f\colon P\rightharpoonup Q$ \emph{partially defined} map we will write $\mathrm{dom}(f)$ for its domain, and will write $f[{\uparrow}x]$ for the image under $f$ of all points in $\mathrm{dom}(f)\cap {\uparrow}x$.
<!-- end notation-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:partial-esakia}
A partial map $f\colon P\to Q$ between finite posets is called a \emph{partial Esakia morphism} if the following conditions hold:\vspace{.2cm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \makebox[3.5cm][l]{(Order-preserving)} If $p,p'\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$ and $p\leq p'$ then $f(p)\leq f(p')$.\vspace{.15cm}
    \item \makebox[3.5cm][l]{(Back-condition)} If $p\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$ and $f(p)\leq q$ then there is some $p'\geq p$ such that $p'\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$ and $f(p')=q$.\vspace{.15cm}
    \item \makebox[3.5cm][l]{(Domain definition)} $p\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$ if and only if $f[{\uparrow}p]={\uparrow}q$ for some $q\in Q$.\vspace{.2cm}
\end{itemize}
Such a map is called \emph{cofinal} if whenever $p\in P$ then there is some $p'\geq p$ such that $p'\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def: closed domain condition}
    Let $Q$ be a finite rooted poset, $P$ a poset, and let $\mathfrak{D}$ be a collection (possibly empty) of antichains of $Q$. A cofinal partial Esakia morphism $f\colon P\to Q$ is said to satisfy the \emph{closed domain condition} (CDC) with respect to $\mathfrak{D}$ if:
    \begin{equation*}
        x\notin \mathrm{dom}(f) \implies \min f[{\uparrow}x]\notin \mathfrak{D}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm: validity of canonical formulas via posets}
    For each finite poset $Q$, and canonical formula $\alpha(P,D)$ we have that $\mathsf{Up}(Q)\nvDash \alpha(P,D)$ if and only if there is an upset $S\subseteq Q$, and an onto cofinal partial Esakia morphism $f\colon S\to P$ satisfying the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{D}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $I$ be an arbitrary set. We denote by
    \begin{equation*}
        M_{I}\coloneqq (\mathcal{P}(I)\setminus \{\varnothing\}, \supseteq);
    \end{equation*}
    we refer to this as a \emph{topless Boolean algebra} or a \emph{Medvedev poset}. We write simply $M_{n}$ for $(\mathcal{P}([n])\setminus \{\varnothing\}, \supseteq)$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop: facts about medvedev posets}
    The following hold of Medvedev posets.
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For each $x,y\in M_{n}$, the union $x\cup y\in M_{n}$, that is, $M_{n}$ is a (meet-)semilattice.
        \item \label{eq: hereditariness of Medvedev posets} For each $x\in M_{n}$, there is some $m\leq n$ such that ${\uparrow}x\cong M_{m}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Given $P$ a finite rooted poset, and $D\subseteq \mathsf{Up}(P)^{2}$ we denote by $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P,D)$ the statement: there is some $n\in \omega$ and a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $M_{n}\rightarrow P$ satisfying the CDC for $\mathfrak{D}_{D}$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm: validity of canonical formula for Medvedev frames}
    For each canonical formula $\alpha(P,D)$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \alpha(P,D)\notin \mathsf{ML} \iff \mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P,D).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P,D)$ holds, then by Theorem \ref{thm: validity of canonical formulas via posets}, 
    for some $n$, $\mathsf{Up}(M_{n})\nvDash \alpha(P,D)$. Conversely, suppose that $\alpha(P,D)\notin \mathsf{ML}$. Since $\mathsf{ML}$ is the logic of the finite Medvedev frames, there is some $M_{n}$ such that $\mathsf{Up}(M_{n})\nvDash \alpha(P,D)$. Thus by the same theorem, there is an upset $S\subseteq M_{n}$ and a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $f\colon S\to P$.

    By surjectivity, let $p\in S$ be such that $f(p)=r$ where $r$ is the root of $P$. Note that by the back condition, then $f{\restriction}_{{\uparrow}p}\colon {\uparrow}p\to P$ is still a cofinal partial Esakia morphism (all conditions are hereditary). Moreover, if for some $x\in {\uparrow}p$, $x\notin \mathrm{dom}(f_{{\uparrow}p})$, then $x\notin \mathrm{dom}(f)$, and so $\min f[{\uparrow}x]\notin \mathfrak{D}_{D}$. By noting that $f[{\uparrow}x]=f_{{\uparrow}p}[{\uparrow}x]$ we conclude that the latter morphism also satisfies the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{D}$. The proof of $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P,D)$ is then concluded by noting that by Proposition \ref{prop: facts about medvedev posets}.\eqref{eq: hereditariness of Medvedev posets}, ${\uparrow}p\cong M_{m}$ for some $m$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
It is well-known that Medvedev posets $M_{n}$ can be interpreted as simplices. For each point $p\in M_{n}$, its depth (i.e., the maximum cardinality of chains above $p$) is the \emph{dimension} of the simplex. We therefore think of the singletons from $M_{n}$ as the \emph{vertices}, the elements of the second layer as the \emph{edges}, the elements of the third layer as the \emph{triangles}, and so on, with each element being understood as a \emph{face}.

This connection and perspective will be employed in the proof below to provide some intuition on the tiling constructions, as many of these constructions can be best understood from the point of view of geometric transformations.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm: infinite frame completeness}
    The logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is complete with respect to $M_{\omega}$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
It was shown in \cite[Theorem 3.2]{Shehtman1986} that if $X$ is a  $T_{1}$ space which is not countably compact, then the logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is complete with respect to the Kripke frame $(\mathsf{Cl}(X),\supseteq)$. By taking the discrete space $\mathbb{N}$ we obtain the result.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Given $P$ a finite rooted poset, and $D\subseteq \mathsf{Up}(P)^{2}$ we denote by $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P,D)$ the statement: there is a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $M_{\omega}\rightarrow P$ satisfying the CDC for $\mathfrak{D}_{D}$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm: validity of canonical formula for skortsov frames}
    For each canonical formula $\alpha(P,D)$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \alpha(P,D)\notin \mathsf{Skvo} \iff \mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{Skvo}}(P,D).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This follows with simpler arguments, as in Theorem \ref{thm: validity of canonical formula for Medvedev frames}, using Theorem \ref{thm: infinite frame completeness}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
A \textit{(Wang) tile} is a tuple $t=(t_W, t_E, t_N, t_S)\in \mathbb{N}^4$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
Given a finite set of tiles $\mathcal{W}\subseteq \mathbb{N}^4$, a \emph{$\mathcal{W}$-tiling} of the plane is a map $\tau: \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}\to \mathcal{W}$ satisfying the horizontal and vertical compatibility conditions for all integers $k,l$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\tau_E(k,l)=\tau_W(k+1,l)$ \hfill (horizontal matching)
        \item $\tau_N(k,l)=\tau_S(k,l+1)$ \hfill (vertical matching)
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
Given a finite set of tiles $\mathcal{W}\subseteq \mathbb{N}^4$, a \emph{periodic $\mathcal{W}$-tiling} consists of a pair of natural numbers $m,n$ and a map $\tau:\mathbb{Z}_m\times \mathbb{Z}_n\to \mathcal{W}$ satisfying the horizontal and vertical compatibility conditions where addition is computed modulo $m$ and $n$ in the first and second coordinate, respectively; in particular, 
    \begin{align*}
        \tau_E(m-1,l)=\tau_W(0,l)\qquad \text{and}\qquad \tau_E(k,n-1)=\tau_W(k,0).
    \end{align*}
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
The ordinary tiling problem is co-r.e.-complete, so undecidable. That is, there is no Turing machine that, when given the specifications of a finite tile set $\mathcal{W}$, decides whether the plane admits a $\mathcal{W}$-tiling.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm: tiling problem is undecidable}
    The periodic tiling problem is r.e.-complete, so undecidable. That is, there is no Turing machine that, when given the specifications of a finite tile set $\mathcal{W}$, decides whether the plane admits a periodic $\mathcal{W}$-tiling.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem: restriction}

For technical reasons we work with the following analogue of the periodic tiling problem: given four finite tile sets $\mathcal{W}_{i,j}$ for $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, decide whether there are is a periodic tiling $\tau:\mathbb{Z}_m\times \mathbb{Z}_n\to \bigcup \mathcal{W}_{i,j}$ with the additional constraint that, for each $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, the restriction of $\tau$ to 
\[
    \{(k,l)\in \mathbb{Z}_m\times \mathbb{Z}_n\mid k = i\mod 2,\; l=j\mod 2\}
\]
is a surjective function onto $\mathcal{W}_{i,j}$.

It is readily verified that this problem is r.e.-complete too. Similarly for the corresponding analogue for the ordinary tiling problem.

For notational convenience we henceforth denote $\mathcal{W}=\bigcup \mathcal{W}_{i,j}$ and typically talk about $\mathcal{W}$-tilings, rather than $\bigcup\mathcal{W}_{i,j}$-tilings.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop: entailment for undecidability}
    Assume that \eqref{eq:keyequation} holds. Then $\mathsf{ML}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{thm: validity of canonical formula for Medvedev frames}, given any finite set of tiles $\mathcal{W}$ as input, whether $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$ holds is reducible to validity of a formula in $\mathsf{ML}$; thus by \eqref{eq:keyequation}, this provides a reduction of the tiling problem to validity in $\mathsf{ML}$, which is not possible by Theorem \ref{thm: tiling problem is undecidable}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
As mentioned in the introduciton,~\cite{Knudstorp2025} proves undecidability for a conservative extension of $\mathsf{Skvo}_\boxempty$. One may therefore wonder whether those results could be extended to cover the present undecidabiliy results. As the reader may guess from the fact that the present paper exists, it is our understanding that they do not.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def: simplex of tiling}
    For each set of Wang tiles, and each periodic tiling $\tau\colon \mathbb{Z}_{m}\times \mathbb{Z}_{k}\to \mathcal{W}$, we define the horizontal sets:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{H}_{0}\coloneqq \{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{m} : n \text{ is even}\} \text{ and } \mathsf{H}_{1}\coloneqq \{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{m} : n \text{ is odd} \};
    \end{equation*}
    similarly we define:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathsf{V}_{0}\coloneqq \{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{k} : n \text{ is even}\} \text{ and } \mathsf{V}_{1}\coloneqq \{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{k} : n \text{ is odd} \}.
    \end{equation*}
    We let $\Omega_{\tau}\coloneqq \mathsf{H}_{0}\sqcup \mathsf{H}_{1}\sqcup \mathsf{V}_{0}\sqcup \mathsf{V}_{1}$, and let $\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)\coloneqq \mathcal{P}(\Omega_{\tau})\setminus \{\varnothing\}$ be the Medvedev frame, called the \emph{simplex of a tiling}  $\tau$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- notation-3: body_md -->
For a point $n\in \Omega_{\tau}$ we let $\mathrm{cor}(n)\in \{\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}\}$ be the unique set to which it belongs. We denote by $\mathrm{cor}[F]$ the usual extension of this to subsets.
<!-- end notation-3 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Of course there are other faces in the simplex whose meaning is less clear: a subset $C\subseteq \mathsf{H}_{0}$ does not obviously have any role in the tiling. Nevertheless, as we will see, such faces play an important role in encoding the possibility of having a periodic tiling.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
Given a set $\mathcal{W}$ of tiles, the poset $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ contains the following points:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item (Horizontal parity points) Two maximal points $\mathsf{H}_{0}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}$;
        \item (Vertical parity points) Two maximal points $\mathsf{V}_{0}$ and $\mathsf{V}_{1}$.
        \item (Horizontal successor points) Three points $\mathsf{R}_{t}$, $\mathsf{R}_{01}$ and $\mathsf{R}_{10}$ that have exactly $\mathsf{H}_{0}$ and $\mathsf{H}_{1}$ as its immediate successors.
        \item (Vertical successor points) Three points $\mathsf{S}_{t}$, $\mathsf{S}_{01}$ and $\mathsf{S}_{10}$ that have exactly $\mathsf{V}_{0}$ and $\mathsf{V}_{1}$ as its immediate successors.
        \item (Tile points) For each $i, j\in \{1,0\}$ and each $t\in \mathcal{W}_{i,j}$ a tile point $\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}$ that has $\mathsf{H}_{i}$ and $\mathsf{V}_{j}$ as its immediate successors.
        \item (Simplex points) For each maximal point $m$, a simplex point $s_{m}$ which has only $m$ as its immediate successor;
        \item (Cut point) For each maximal point $m$, a cut point $c_{m}$ containing only $s_{m}$ as its successor.
        \item (Root) A root element $r$ which is below all other points.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def: folding morphism}
    Given a tiling $\tau$ of the set of tiles $\mathcal{W}$, we define the folding map $f_{\tau}\colon \mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)\to P_{\mathcal{W}}$ by induction, as follows:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item (Singleton) For each singleton $\{n\}$, $f_{\tau}(\{n\})=\mathrm{cor}(n)$;
        \item For each doubleton $D=\{n,n'\}$:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item If $f_{\tau}(\{n\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$ and $f_{\tau}(\{n'\})=\mathsf{H}_{1}$, then:
            \begin{enumerate}
                \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{R}_{01}$ if $n'=n+1$ $\mod {m}$;
                \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{R}_{10}$ if $n=n'+1 \mod {m}$;
            \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{R}_{t}$ otherwise.\end{enumerate}
            
        \item If $f_{\tau}(\{n\})=\mathsf{V}_{0}$ and $f_{\tau}(\{n'\})=\mathsf{V}_{1}$, then:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{S}_{01}$ if $n'=n+1 \mod {k}$;
            \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{S}_{10}$ if $n=n'+1 \mod {k}$;
        \item $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{S}_{t}$ otherwise.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item If $f_{\tau}(\{n\})=\mathsf{H}_{i}$ and $f_{\tau}(\{n'\})=\mathsf{V}_{j}$ then let $t\coloneqq \tau(n,n')$ and map $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}$.
\end{enumerate}
\item If $F\subseteq \Omega$ is any face such that $|F|>1$ (including a doubleton), such that $|\mathrm{cor}[F]|=T$ for $T\in \{\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}\}$, then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $F$ contains all points sent to $T$, then $f_{\tau}(F)=c_{T}$;
    \item Otherwise $f_{\tau}(F)=d_{T}$.
\end{enumerate}  
        \item $f_{\tau}(\Omega)=r$.
        \item $f_{\tau}$ is not defined anywhere else on the domain of $\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The role of the simplex and cut points is more involved, and is best understood by thinking of the map $f_{\tau}$ as providing a \emph{coloring} to the simplex, with the top labels $\mathsf{H}_{i}$ and $\mathsf{V}_{j}$ serving as the colors.

    Under this reading, the points which get mapped to the \emph{simplex} point are exactly the monochromatic simplices which are neither maximal nor degenerate. Those which get sent to the \emph{cut} point are the maximal monochromatic simplices. 
    
    Having such points buys us expressive power in the tiling: since we can talk about monochromatic faces, if we ensure certain faces \emph{omit} any non-trivial monochromatic simplex, this can force us to identify certain points. On the other hand,    
    since we can talk about the largest monochromatic simplex, we can force the existence of points within a given prescribed successor relation.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop: domain definition}
    For each set $\mathcal{W}$ of tiles, $\tau$ a tiling and $F\in \mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)$ we have that $F\in \mathrm{dom}(f_{\tau})$ if and only if one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $|F|\leq 2$;
        \item $|F|>2$ and $\mathrm{cor}[F]$ is a singleton.
        \item $F=\Omega$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop: folding map partial esakia}
    For each set $\mathcal{W}$ of tiles, and $\tau\colon \mathbb{Z}_{m}\times\mathbb{Z}_{k}\to \mathcal{W}$ a tiling where $m,k\geq 6$\footnote{As remarked in the next section, this assumption is purely technical and can be removed without affecting the core argument of the proof.}, the folding map $f_{\tau}$ is a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $P_{\mathcal{W}}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The fact that the map is onto follows from an easy case analysis, noting that the simplex $\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)$ must contain points in all the given positions, since $m,k\geq 6$, and since, by Remark \ref{rem: restriction}, only the tile points which arise in the tiling $\tau$ are put in the poset $\mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)$. 

Moreover, the map is order-preserving and satisfies the back-condition. The domain condition follows at once from Proposition \ref{prop: domain definition}. Finally, the map is cofinal, since all of the singletons are in the domain.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Proposition \ref{prop: folding map partial esakia} and its elementary proof is one of the key advantages of working with Zakharyaschev's canonical formulas: instead of having to define the function $f_{\tau}$ on a \emph{whole structure}, it is possible to define it only on the parts which carry the most relevant geometric information.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex: missing compatibility}
Consider a tripleton $\{n,n',n''\}$. By focusing on its face poset we obtain, for example, the picture of Figure \ref{fig:compatibilitytriple}:

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering

    \begin{tikzpicture}
        \node at (0,0) {$\bullet$};
        \node at (0,0.3) {$n$};
        \node at (-1.5,-2.5) {$\bullet$};
        \node at (-1.8,-2.8) {$n'$};
        \node at (1.5,-2.5) {$\bullet$};
        \node at (1.8,-2.8) {$n''$};

        \draw (0,0) -- (-1.5,-2.5) -- (1.5,-2.5) -- (0,0);

        \node at (0,-3) {$R_{10}$};

        \node at (-1.5,-1.3) {$T_{t,1,0}$};

        \node at (1.5,-1.3) {$T_{t',0,0}$};
\end{tikzpicture}    \caption{Compatibility triple}
    \label{fig:compatibilitytriple}
\end{figure}
Given the way the map $f_{\tau}$ was designed, we know that $n''=n'+1$, and so the horizontal coordinates align, and moreover, $\tau(n',n)=t$ whilst $\tau(n'',n)=t'$. However, there is an obvious additional requirement: $t$ should be \emph{compatible} with $t'$, i.e.
\begin{equation*}
    t_E=t'_W,
\end{equation*}
and similarly for vertical compatibility.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def: tiling domain}
    Given a set $\mathcal{W}$ of tiles, we define the following closed domain $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$ of $P_{\mathcal{W}}$:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item\label{eq:maximalcuts} (Maximal cuts) For $(A,B)$ one of the six pairs:
    \begin{equation*}
        (\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1}),(\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}),(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{0}),(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}),(\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{0}),(\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{1}),
    \end{equation*}
    we add the pair $(\{A\},\{B\})$.
        \item (Successor cuts) Given a pair $(S,T)$, from amongst:
        \begin{equation*}
            (\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1}),(\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{H}_{0}),(\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}),(\mathsf{V}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{0}),
        \end{equation*}
        we use the following definitions:

\begin{table}[h]
    \centering
\begin{tabular}
{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Pair & Target \(T\) & Non-matching \(N\) & Matching \(Q\)\\
\midrule
$(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})$ & \(\mathsf H_1\)
  & \(\{R_{00},R_{10}\}\) & \(R_{01}\)\\
$(\mathsf{H}_{1},\mathsf{H}_{0})$ & \(\mathsf H_0\)
  & \(\{R_{00},R_{01}\}\) & \(R_{10}\)\\
$(\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1})$ & \(\mathsf V_1\)
  & \(\{S_{00},S_{10}\}\) & \(S_{01}\)\\
$(\mathsf{V}_{1},\mathsf{V}_{0})$ & \(\mathsf V_0\)
  & \(\{S_{00},S_{01}\}\) & \(S_{10}\)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
    \caption{Successor cut data}
    \label{tab:successorcutdata}
\end{table}

Using this table, we define the following sets:        \begin{equation*}
            A_{(S,T)}=P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (N_{(S,T)}\cup \{Q_{(S,T)},r\}) \text{ and } B_{(S,T)}=P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (\{Q_{(S,T)},c_{T},r\}).
        \end{equation*}
        and we put the pair $(A_{(S,T)},B_{(S,T)})\in D_{\mathcal{W}}$.
  \item (Horizontal compatibility cuts) For each $i,j\in\{0,1\}$ and each $t\in \mathcal{W}_{i,j}$, let $\mathrm{HComp}(t)=\{t'\in \mathcal{W}_{1-i,j} : t_E=t'_W\}$, and shorten $\mathsf{R}_{0}\coloneqq \mathsf{R}_{01}$ and $\mathsf{R}_{1}\coloneqq \mathsf{R}_{10}$. Then define:
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}\coloneqq \{\mathsf{T}_{1-i,j,t'} \mid t'\in \mathrm{HComp}(t)\}.
        \end{equation*}
        and define the following sets:
        \begin{align*}
            C_{i,j,t}&\coloneqq P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (\{\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t},s_{\mathsf{H}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{H}_{i}},r\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t})\\
            D_{i,j,t} &\coloneqq P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (\{\mathsf{R}_{i},s_{\mathsf{H}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{H}_{i}},r\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}).
        \end{align*}
        and we put the pair $(C_{i,j,t},D_{i,j,t})\in D_{\mathcal{W}}$.
\item (Vertical compatibility cuts) For each $i,j\in\{0,1\}$ and each $t\in \mathcal{W}_{i,j}$, let $\mathrm{VComp}(t)=\{t'\in \mathcal{W}_{i,1-j} \mid t_N=t'_S\}$, and shorten $\mathsf{S}_{0}\coloneqq \mathsf{S}_{01}$ and $\mathsf{S}_{1}\coloneqq \mathsf{R}_{10}$. Then define:
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}\coloneqq \{\mathsf{T}_{i,1-j,t'} : t'\in \mathrm{VComp}(t)\}.
        \end{equation*}
        and define the following sets:
        \begin{align*}
            C_{i,j,t}&\coloneqq P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (\{\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t},s_{\mathsf{V}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{V}_{i},r}\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t})\\
            D_{i,j,t} &\coloneqq P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (\{\mathsf{S}_{i},s_{\mathsf{V}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{V}_{i}},r\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}),
        \end{align*}
    and we put the pair $(C_{i,j,t},D_{i,j,t})\in D_{\mathcal{W}}$.
\end{enumerate}

    We then set $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$ as in Definition \ref{def: closed domain condition}, i.e., adding to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$ all antichains which are contained in the union of one of the pairs, and have non-empty intersection with both sets.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem: cut calculations}
    Given any set of tiles $\mathcal{W}$ the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  For each pair of \emph{successor cuts} $(S,T)$, we have that:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $A_{(S,T)}\setminus B_{(S,T)}=\{c_{T}\}$;
            \item $B_{(S,T)}\setminus A_{(S,T)}=N_{(S,T)}$;
            \item $P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (A_{(S,T)}\cup B_{(S,T)})=\{r,Q_{(S,T)}\}$.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item\label{eq:horizontal cut calculations} For each tile $t\in \mathcal{W}$, and each pair $(C_{i,j,t},D_{i,j,t})$ of \emph{horizontal compatibility cuts} we have:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $C_{i,j,t}\setminus D_{i,j,t}=\{\mathsf{R}_{i}\}$;
            \item $D_{i,j,t}\setminus C_{i,j,t}=\{\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}\}$;
            \item $P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t})=\{r,s_{\mathsf{H}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{H}_{i}}\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}$.
        \end{enumerate}
        \item For each tile $t\in \mathcal{W}$, and each pair $(C_{i,j,t},D_{i,j,t})$ of \emph{vertical compatibility cuts} we have:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item $C_{i,j,t}\setminus D_{i,j,t}=\{\mathsf{S}_{i}\}$;
            \item $D_{i,j,t}\setminus C_{i,j,t}=\{\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}\}$;
            \item $P_{\mathcal{W}}\setminus (C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t})=\{r,s_{\mathsf{V}_{i}},c_{\mathsf{V}_{i}}\}\cup \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let us again return to the triangle of Figure \ref{fig:compatibilitytriple}. We will show, simply from the fact that $f_{\tau}$ satisfies the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$, that $t$ and $t'$ are compatible. For this purpose, consider the tripleton:
    \begin{equation*}
        F=\{n,n',n''\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Given what we assume of this face, and the way that $f_{\tau}$ was defined, we have that $F\notin \mathrm{dom}(f_{\tau})$. On the other hand, by assumption, we have:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq: image of the map}
        f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]=\{\mathsf{R}_{10},\mathsf{T}_{t,1,0},\mathsf{T}_{t',0,0}\}.
    \end{equation}
    By construction this is an antichain, and we have by the assumption of the CDC that it does not belong to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$. Now assume, towards a contradiction, that $t'\notin \mathrm{HComp}(t)$ i.e., the tile is not horizontally compatible. Then $\mathsf{T}_{t',0,0}\notin \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}$, and so by Lemma \ref{lem: cut calculations}.\eqref{eq:horizontal cut calculations}:
    \begin{equation*}
        f[{\uparrow}F]\subseteq C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t}.
    \end{equation*}
    On the other hand, by the same calculations, one sees, upon inspecting \eqref{eq: image of the map} that we have $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]\cap (C_{i,j,t}\setminus D_{i,j,t})\neq \emptyset$ and $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]\cap (D_{i,j,t}\setminus C_{i,j,t})\neq \emptyset$. This is a contradiction to the construction of $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$, since all antichains contained in the union and having non-empty intersection with both upsets. By reductio, we conclude that $t'$ is horizontally compatible.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop: folding map satisfies CDC}
    The map $f_{\tau}$ is a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ satisfying the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The fact that $f_{\tau}$ is a cofinal partial Esakia morphism and onto was shown in Proposition \ref{prop: folding map partial esakia}. We thus focus on proving the CDC.

    So assume that $F\in \mathcal{T}_{\tau}(\Omega)$ is a face such that $F\notin \mathrm{dom}(f_{\tau})$. Thus, by Proposition \ref{prop: domain definition} we know that $F$ is not the root, $|F|>2$ and there exist at least two points $n,n'$ with different coordinate-parity.      The proof proceeds by cases, depending on the kind of cut considered.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item (Horizontal cuts) Suppose towards a contradiction that $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]$ is an antichain contained in $C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t}$, and intersecting each of the two sets. The latter condition means that there are $D_{i}\subseteq F$ such that $f_{\tau}(D_{i})=\mathsf{R}_{i}$, and $D_{t}\subseteq F$ such that $f_{\tau}(D_{t})=\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}$. Say that $D_{i}=\{n_{0},n_{1}\}$. Assume without loss of generality that  $f_{\tau}(\{n_{0}\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$ and $f_{\tau}(\{n_{1}\})=\mathsf{H}_{1}$. The construction of $f_{\tau}$ then tells us  that $n_{1}=n_{0}+1$. 
        
        On the other hand, by definition of $D_{t}=\{n_{2},n_{3}\}$ where $f_{\tau}(\{n_{2}\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$ ($i=0$ by the assumption on $\mathsf{R}_{i}=\mathsf{R}_{01}$ made above), and $f_{\tau}(\{n_{3}\})=\mathsf{V}_{j}$. 

        However, note that by Lemma \ref{lem: cut calculations}, $s_{\mathsf{H}_{i}}\notin C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t}$. Since by assumption we must have $f_{\tau}(\{n_{0}\})=f_{\tau}(\{n_{2}\})$ we conclude:
        \begin{equation*}
            n_{0}=n_{2}
        \end{equation*}
        in other words, the \emph{simplex point being excluded ensures the square becomes a triangle along the $i$-coordinate}.
        
        We thus consider the tripleton:
        \begin{equation*}
            F_{0}=\{n_{0},n_{1},n_{3}\}\subseteq F.
        \end{equation*}
        The situation obtained now is analogous to that from Example \ref{ex: missing compatibility}. Namely: $f_{\tau}(\{n_{0},n_{1}\})=\mathsf{R}_{01}$, and $f_{\tau}(\{n_{0},n_{3}\})=\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t}$.  So we can ask what is $f_{\tau}(\{n_{1},n_{3}\})$ is. By construction on the tiling, we have that $\tau(n_{0},n_{3})=t$ and $\tau(n_{1},n_{3})=t'$, and since $n_{1}=n_{0}+1$, we have that
        \begin{equation*}
            \mathrm{w}(t)=\mathrm{e}(t').
        \end{equation*}
        Thus $f_{\tau}(\{n_{1},n_{3}\})=\mathsf{T}_{1,j,t'}$, and by construction, $\mathsf{T}_{1,j,t'}\in \mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}$. But this is a contradiction, since by Lemma \ref{lem: cut calculations}, $\mathrm{G}_{i,j,t}\cap (C_{i,j,t}\cup D_{i,j,t})=\varnothing$. This is a contradiction to our assumption on $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]$ being contained in the union.
        
        An entirely similar case follows if we assume that $i=1$.
        \item (Vertical cuts) The proof is entirely analogous to the case for horizontal cuts.
        \item (Successor cuts) Suppose that $(S,T)$ is a pair of successor cuts, say, without loss of generality that it is $(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})$. Assume that $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]$ is an antichain contained in $A_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\cup B_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}$, and intersecting each of them as needed. Note that then $F_{1}\subseteq F$ is a face such that every odd number from $\mathbb{Z}_{m}$ is contained there (by definition of when $f_{\tau}(F_{1})=c_{\mathsf{H}_{1}}$). On the other hand there is a doubleton $D\subseteq F$ such that $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{R}_{00}$ or $f_{\tau}(D)=\mathsf{R}_{10}$, and so there is a point $n\in F$ such that $f_{\tau}(\{n\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$. Let $n'$ be arbitrary such that $n'=n+1\mod \mathbb{Z}_{m}$; then $n'\in F$ by our assumption on $F_{1}$. Thus we have that:
        \begin{equation*}
            D_{0}=\{n,n'\}\subseteq F,
        \end{equation*}
        and by definition $f_{\tau}(D_{0})=\mathsf{R}_{01}$, whilst by assumption, $\mathsf{R}_{01}\notin A_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\cup B_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}$. This is a contradiction to $f_{\tau}[{\uparrow}F]$ being contained in the union.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor: Tiling implies Medvedev covers}
    Whenever $\mathcal{W}$ is a set of tiles which tiles periodically, then $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$ holds.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem: well-defined induced tiling}
    For each $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, we have that
    \begin{equation*}
        f(\{a,b\})\in \{\mathsf{T}_{i,j,t} : i,j\in \{0,1\},t\in \mathcal{W}\},
    \end{equation*}
    i.e., $f$ is defined at the doubleton, and it maps to one of the tile points.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Note that if $f$ is defined on $\{a,b\}$, then to satisfy order-preservation, it must map to the tile points. If $\{a,b\}\notin \mathrm{dom}(f)$, since $f$ satisfies the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$, we obtain that $f[{\uparrow}\{a,b\}]\notin \mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$ -- a contradiction to the latter containing all antichains in the maximal cuts (see Definition \ref{def: tiling domain}.\eqref{eq:maximalcuts}). By reductio, we conclude that $\{a,b\}\in \mathrm{dom}(f)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem: doubletons are in the domain}
Let
\begin{equation*}
    A\coloneqq \max (f^{-1}[\{\mathsf{H}_{0}\}]) \text{ and } B\coloneqq \max(f^{-1}[\{\mathsf{H}_{1}\}]).
\end{equation*}
    Then for each $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, we have that
    \begin{equation*}
        f(\{a,b\})\in \{\mathsf{R}_{01}, \mathsf{R}_{10}, \mathsf{R}_{t}\},
    \end{equation*}
    i.e., $f$ is defined at the doubleton, and it maps to one of the horizontal successor points. 

    Similarly, let 
    \begin{equation*}
    A\coloneqq \max (f^{-1}[\{\mathsf{V}_{0}\}]) \text{ and } B\coloneqq \max(f^{-1}[\{\mathsf{V}_{1}\}]).
\end{equation*}
Then for each $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, we have that
    \begin{equation*}
        f(\{a,b\})\in \{\mathsf{S}_{01}, \mathsf{S}_{10}, \mathsf{S}_{t}\},
    \end{equation*}
    i.e., $f$ is defined at the doubleton, and it maps to one of the vertical successor points.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem: successor lemma}
    For each $a\in A$ and $b\in B$, if $f(\{a\})=\mathsf{H}_{i}$, there is some $a'\in A$ such that $f(\{a'\})=\mathsf{H}_{1-i}$, and such that:
    \begin{equation*}
        f(\{a,a'\})=\mathsf{R}_{i1-i}.
    \end{equation*}   
    Similarly for each $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ such that $f(\{b\})=\mathsf{V}_{j}$, there exists some $b'\in B$ such that $f(\{b'\})=\mathsf{V}_{1-j}$, and
    \begin{equation*}
        f(\{b,b'\})=\mathsf{S}_{j1-j}.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The two statements follow from very similar arguments, using vertical instead of horizontal cuts and successors. We show the case for horizontal successors in detail.
    
    Without loss of generality assume that $f(\{a\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$. We once again use the cut points: since $f$ is onto, pick $F\in M_{n}$ such that $f(F)=c_{\mathsf{H}_{1}}$. Then look at:
    \begin{equation*}
        F'\coloneqq F\cup \{a\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Note that since $f(F)=c_{\mathsf{H}_{1}}$ and $f(\{a\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$, and the map is order-preserving, if $F'$ was in the domain, we would have to have $f(F')=r$; but since $f$ is a p-morphism, then $F'$ would have to contain points mapping to $\mathsf{V}_{0},\mathsf{V}_{1}$ -- a contradiction. So we obtain that $F'\notin \mathrm{dom}(f)$. Because $f$ satisfies the CDC with respect to the successor cut $(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})$, this means that:
    \begin{equation*}
        \min f[{\uparrow}F']\notin \mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}.
    \end{equation*}
    Take $e\in F$, then $f[\{e\}]=\mathsf{H}_{1}$; thus by Lemma \ref{lem: doubletons are in the domain}, we know that $f[\{e,a\}]\in \{\mathsf{R}_{t},\mathsf{R}_{10},\mathsf{R}_{01}\}$. If $f[\{e,a\}]=\mathsf{R}_{01}$, we are done, so suppose not. Then we have:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $f[{\uparrow}F']\cap A_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\setminus B_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\neq \emptyset$, since $f(F)=c_{T}$, and $F'\supseteq F$;
        \item $f[{\uparrow}F']\cap B_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\setminus A_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\neq \emptyset$, since one of $\mathsf{R}_{t}$ and $\mathsf{R}_{10}$ is by hypothesis there.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Since we have that $\min f[{\uparrow}F']\notin \mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$ this can only happen if $\min f[{\uparrow}F']\nsubseteq A_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}\cup B_{(\mathsf{H}_{0},\mathsf{H}_{1})}$. Thus either $r\in \min f[{\uparrow}F']$ -- which we have ruled out -- or $\mathsf{R}_{01}\in  f[{\uparrow}F']$. By taking $F'\supseteq E$, where $E$ is any face such that $f(E)=\mathsf{R}_{01}$, we see that there must be a point $a'\in E$, and by order-preservation, and the fact that $E\supseteq \{a,a'\}$, we get that $f(\{a,a'\})=\mathsf{R}_{01}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem: key compatibility lemma}
    Let $a,a'\in A$ be such that $f(\{a,a'\})=\mathsf{R}_{i1-i}$. Then for any $b$, we have:
\begin{equation*}
        \mathrm{e}(t_{a,b})=\mathrm{w}(t_{a',b}).
    \end{equation*}
    Similarly, whenever $b,b'\in B$ are such that $f(\{b,b'\})=\mathsf{S}_{j1-j}$, then for any $a\in A$, we have:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathrm{n}(t_{a,b})=\mathrm{s}(t_{a,b'}).
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Once again we show the case for horizontal compatibility, the vertical one following by exactly the same arguments. 

    We need to show that $t_{a,b}$ and $t_{a,b'}$ are compatible. For this purpose, we once again consider the tripleton:
    \begin{equation*}
        E=\{a,a',b\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Note that $f(\{a\})=\mathsf{H}_{0}$, $f(\{a'\})=\mathsf{H}_{1}$ and $f(\{b\})=\mathsf{V}_{j}$, so $E\notin \mathrm{dom}(f)$ by the same arguments as given in Lemma \ref{lem: successor lemma} for why $F'\notin \mathrm{dom}(f)$. Since $f$ satisfies the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$, we have that:
    \begin{equation*}
        f[{\uparrow}E]\notin \mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}} \text{ and } f[{\uparrow}E]=\{\mathsf{R}_{01},\mathsf{T}_{0,j,t_{a,b}},\mathsf{T}_{1,j,t_{a',b}}\}.
    \end{equation*}
    Once again, by Lemma \ref{lem: cut calculations}, we have that $f[{\uparrow}E]\cap C_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\setminus D_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\neq \varnothing$, and we have likewise that $f[{\uparrow}E]\cap D_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\setminus C_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\neq \varnothing$. Thus $f[{\uparrow}E]\nsubseteq C_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\cup D_{0,j,t_{a,b}}$, which means that:
    \begin{equation*}
        f[{\uparrow}E]\cap \mathrm{G}_{0,j,t_{a,b}}\neq \varnothing.
    \end{equation*}
    This means that $\mathsf{T}_{1,j,t_{a',b}}\in \mathrm{G}_{0,j,t_{a,b}}$; by construction of the latter set, we then have that $\mathrm{e}(t_{a,b})=\mathrm{w}(t_{a',b})$, which was to show.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop: induced tiling function is a periodic tiling}
    The function $\tau$ defines a periodic tiling of the plane.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Pick $a_{0},b_{0}$ two arbitrary elements. Using Lemma \ref{lem: successor lemma}, we pick a chain of successors:
    \begin{equation*}
        a_{0},a_{1},\dots,a_{n},\dots
    \end{equation*}
    Since $M_{n}$ is finite, and the points $a_{i}$ as above are maximal points of $M_{n}$, we have that eventually there must be a period -- and thus we may assume that in fact $a_{0},\dots,a_{m}$ is the first such chain. Note moreover that on the $b_{0}$-row, this provides a tiling by Lemma \ref{lem: key compatibility lemma}. 

    Now pick $b_{1}$ some successor of $b_{0}$. Then note that again by Lemma \ref{lem: key compatibility lemma}, the tiles $\tau(a_{i},b_{0})$ and $\tau(a_{i},{b_{1}})$ will be vertically compatible, whilst the tiles $\tau(a_{i},b_{1})$ and $\tau(a_{i+1},b_{1})$ will be horizontally compatible. Proceeding in this way, we again obtain a period $b_{1},\dots,b_{k}$, where all tiles are pairwise compatible as needed.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor: Medvedev covers implies tiling}
    For each set of tiles $\mathcal{W}$, whenever $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$, we have that $\mathcal{W}$ tiles the plane periodically.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm: medvedev's logic is undecidable}
    Medvedev's logic $\mathsf{ML}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{prop: entailment for undecidability}, we have that proving \eqref{eq:keyequation} shows that $\mathsf{ML}$ is undecidable. The left to right direction is Corollary \ref{cor: Tiling implies Medvedev covers}, whilst the right to left direction is Corollary \ref{cor: Medvedev covers implies tiling}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop: equation and skvortsov undecidability}
    Assume that \eqref{eq:secondkeyequation} holds. Then $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop: folding map satisfies CDC infinite}
    If $\tau$ is an arbitrary tiling map $f_{\tau}$ is a cofinal partial Esakia morphism onto $P_{\mathcal{W}}$ satisfying the CDC with respect to $\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}}$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We can repeat the proofs of Proposition \ref{prop: folding map partial esakia} and Proposition \ref{prop: folding map satisfies CDC} verbatim, except one swaps periodic tiling for usual tiling.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor: Tiling implies skortsov covers}
    Whenever $\mathcal{W}$ is a set of tiles which tiles the plane, then $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{Skvo}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$ holds.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop: induced tiling function is a tiling}
    The function $\tau$ defines a tiling of the plane.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We proceed as in Proposition \ref{prop: induced tiling function is a periodic tiling}. By picking $a_{0}$ and $b_{0}$ arbitrary, we produce an enumeration:
    \begin{equation*}
        A_{0}\coloneqq (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n},\dots,)
    \end{equation*}
    and likewise, enumerate,
    \begin{equation*}
        B_{0}\coloneqq (b_{0},b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n},\dots)
    \end{equation*}
    where we construct the enumeration row-by-row using Lemma \ref{lem: successor lemma}. Lemma \ref{lem: key compatibility lemma} ensures that the pairs are always compatible, meaning that restricting to the domain $A_{0}\times B_{0}$ obtains a tiling of the plane, as desired.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor: skortsov covers implies tiling}
    For each set of tiles $\mathcal{W}$, whenever $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{Skvo}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$, we have that $\mathcal{W}$ tiles the plane.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm: skortov is undecidable}
    Skvortsov's logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is undecidable.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{prop: equation and skvortsov undecidability}, we have that $\mathsf{Skvo}$ being undecidable is equivalent to \eqref{eq:secondkeyequation}. The left to right direction is supplied by Corollary \ref{cor: skortsov covers implies tiling}, whilst the right to left is given by Corollary \ref{cor: skortsov covers implies tiling}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor: separation of skvortsov and medvedev}
    The logic $\mathsf{Skvo}$ is a proper sublogic of $\mathsf{ML}$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{W}$ be a finite set of Wang tiles which is known to \emph{only tile the plane} aperiodically\footnote{For an example of such a tile, see \cite{Jeandel2021}, which also contains extensive discussion on such tile sets.}. By Corollary \ref{cor: Medvedev covers implies tiling}, we have that $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{ML}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$ fails, and thus, by Thoerem \ref{thm: validity of canonical formula for Medvedev frames}, $\alpha(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})\in \mathsf{ML}$. On the other hand, by Corollary \ref{cor: skortsov covers implies tiling}, we have that $\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathsf{Skvo}}(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})$, which 
    by Theorem \ref{thm: validity of canonical formula for skortsov frames}, means that $\alpha(P_{\mathcal{W}},\mathfrak{D}_{\mathcal{W}})\notin \mathsf{Skvo}$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- problem-7: body_md -->
Is $Y_{\mathsf{ML}}$ equal to $\mathsf{ML}$? Is it is equal to $\mathsf{Skvo}$? Is it equal to $Y_{\mathsf{Skvo}}$? Is this logic decidable?
<!-- end problem-7 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
A superintuitionistic logic $L$ is said to have \emph{degree of the finite model property $\kappa$} for $\kappa$ a cardinal if and only if the following set has cardinality $\kappa$\footnote{Note that it was proven in \cite[Thm.~3.8,Rem.~3.9]{cardinalitiesdegreeoffmp} that for the degree of FMP (and many other measures in lattices of varieties), the only possible infinite cardinals are $\aleph_{0}$ and $2^{\aleph_{0}}$.}:
    \begin{equation*}
        \mathrm{deg}_{\mathsf{FMP}}(L)\coloneqq |\{L_{0}\in \mathrm{Ext}(\mathsf{IPC}) : L_{0} \text{ has the same finite frames as } L\}|.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- problem-8: body_md -->
Characterize the degree of FMP of $\mathsf{ML}$.
<!-- end problem-8 -->
<!-- problem-9: body_md -->
Does there exist a finite poset $F$ with a top element such that $\mathsf{TLP}_{\mathbf{F}}$ is decidable?
<!-- end problem-9 -->
<!-- problem-10: body_md -->
Is $\mathsf{ML}$ the unique Friedman logic (both structurally complete and with the disjunction property)?
<!-- end problem-10 -->
<!-- problem-11: body_md -->
Is $\mathsf{Cheq}$ recursively axiomatizable? Equivalently, is $\mathsf{Cheq}$ decidable?
<!-- end problem-11 -->
<!-- problem-12: body_md -->
\label{prob: realizability logic}
    Is the logic $\mathsf{Realiz}$ decidable? Does it have the finite model property?
<!-- end problem-12 -->
